overview: Nine Department of State “List of Papers” index sheets summarize correspondence filed from 1940 through 1943 concerning Japanese merchant shipping. The entries trace commercial services and shipbuilding intelligence, Japanese government requisition and diversion of vessels, cargo claims involving American and Dutch interests, Panama Canal movements, and requests for immunity from legal process for government-controlled ships. Recurring cases concern the TATUTA/TATSUTA MARU and SANYO MARU, while later entries reflect wartime losses, shipping shortages, and intelligence gathering.

subfiles.title: List of papers: shipping restrictions and consular reports, entries 550–552
subfiles.about: Indexes early 1940 reports on Shandong coastal restrictions and Japanese shipping at Canton, Whampoa, and Kobe.
subfiles.summary: Lists 1940s entries on abolished Shandong shipping restrictions, Japanese military transports at Canton, and new Kobe reporting difficulties.

subfiles.title: List of papers: Japanese services, shipbuilding, and tonnage acquisition, entries 553–562
subfiles.about: Indexes reports on Japanese shipbuilding data, overseas steamship services, and efforts to acquire additional tonnage.
subfiles.summary: Lists entries on nonavailable Japanese shipbuilding figures, Latin American services, Panama routing, China-financed vessel acquisitions, and new Haiphong-Japan service.

subfiles.title: List of papers: cargo appeals for Tatsuta Maru and Haiki Maru
subfiles.about: Indexes commercial requests to unload American-owned cargo from Japanese vessels on the Pacific Coast.
subfiles.summary: Lists cargo-unloading appeals for the Tatuta and Haiki Maru at San Francisco, and denials of oil-loading rumors at Houston.

subfiles.title: List of papers: Panama Canal delays and requisitioned Japanese ships
subfiles.about: Indexes reports on Japanese shipping to South America, Canal passage delays, and requisitioned vessels.
subfiles.summary: Lists reports on Japanese steamers held at the Panama Canal, requisitioned ships Kongo and Ayumasan Maru, and Army shipping report.

subfiles.title: List of papers: requisitions, diversions, and detentions, entries 641–647
subfiles.about: Indexes policy correspondence on Japanese ship requisitions, cargo diversions, and the detention or treatment of vessels and passengers.
subfiles.summary: Lists entries on detained Tatuta Maru passengers, Japanese steamers held at Cristóbal, diverted cargoes, and Japanese vessels in Australian waters.

subfiles.title: List of papers: immunity and port entry for government-controlled ships
subfiles.about: Indexes legal correspondence concerning immunity, requisition dates, and the TATSUTA MARU’s entry into Balboa.
subfiles.summary: Lists entries on Tatuta Maru's legal immunity, requisition dates for named vessels, and Tatsuta Maru's approved Balboa entry.

subfiles.title: List of papers: Sanyo Maru cargo and wartime shipping intelligence, entries 675–688
subfiles.about: Indexes investigations of SANYO MARU cargo alongside reports on Japanese shipbuilding, requisitioned ships, and wartime fleet conditions.
subfiles.summary: Lists entries on Sanyo Maru's 1940 New York cargo, Dutch claims, the requisitioned Tatuta Maru, and wartime Nagasaki shipping intelligence.

subfiles.title: List of papers: Dutch claims to Sanyo Maru cargo, entries 689–695
subfiles.about: Indexes Treasury and Netherlands Embassy correspondence about SANYO MARU cargo and Chinese intelligence on Japanese merchant vessels.
subfiles.summary: Lists Treasury-Netherlands exchanges over Sanyo Maru cargo in New York, Chinese shipping data, and Dutch claims to specific cargo lots.

subfiles.title: List of papers: cargo disposition, Tatsuta Maru sinking, and shipping shortage, entries 697–704
subfiles.about: Indexes final SANYO MARU cargo inquiries, a Japanese shipping-company bankruptcy, and wartime reports on the TATUTA MARU and Japan’s shipping shortage.
subfiles.summary: Lists continued Sanyo Maru cargo investigation, a shipping-company bankruptcy, Tatuta Maru's October sinking off Chefoo, and a Guardian shortage article.

interest: Shows 1940-43 shift from routine Japanese shipping monitoring to cargo seizures and wartime intelligence, via Sanyo and Tatsuta Maru cases.
